newsitem.title: BELGIUM: More reform needed before EMU, EU tells applicants.
newsitem.headline: More reform needed before EMU, EU tells applicants.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday that applicant countries from eastern and central Europe could probably not join monetary union at the same time as becoming members of the 15-nation European Union.
The EU executive underlined that further progress in structural reforms was necessary before they would be able to "maintain sufficient macroeconomic stability in the long run."

"With respect to the aim of economic and monetary union, it is unlikely that the applicants will be able to join the euro area immediately upon accession," it said in a report on which East European countries should be asked to membershiop talks.

However, they were expected to take part in an EU exchange rate mechanism and avoid excessive exchange rate changes. The Commission also said new member states should have completed the liberalisation of capital movements.

Even if they would not be immediately ready for economic and monetary union (EMU), the Commission said new members would have to adopt rules included in the second phase of economic and monetary union, which started on January 1, 1994.

"This implies central bank independence, coordination of economic policies (national convergence programmes, multilateral surveillance, excessive deficit procedure,...), and adherence to the relevant provisions of the stability and growth pact."

"New member states will forego any direct central bank financing of public sector deficits as well as priviliged access of public authorities to financial institutions," it added in its so-called Agenda 2000 document.
The stability and growth pact is designed to ensure that countries maintain fiscal discipline also after the launch of the third phase of monetary union on January 1, 1999.

In the document, the Commission unveiled plans to embrace five members of the former Communist bloc, saying Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Estonia and Slovenia should be invited to begin EU membership talks along with Cyprus next year.

The Commission also said that although Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Bulgaria and Romania had not made the grade, they should be kept in what amounts to a waiting room where they can prepare for membership at their own pace.

According to the Commission's documents on the applicants, the five countries which are due to start EU membership talks next year have made progress in reducing budget deficits, but inflation remains far above the EU level.

Poland, for example, has a budget deficit of less than three percent, the limit set in the EU's Maastricht treaty for EMU, but it had an inflation rate of 19.9 percent in 1996, compared with the EU annual rate of 1.5 percent in May.
Currently, the applicants pursue different foreign exchange policies. Estonia, for example, has a currency board while the Polish zloty is gradually devalued in a crawling peg system.
In May, the Czech central bank was forced to let the crown float following a speculative assault on the currency.
